docs.title: wavio
docs.text:
Peak-based audio fingerprinting. Zero overhead. Written in Rust.

Identify audio tracks in microseconds — no ML, no embeddings, just spectral peaks and combinatorial hashing.

  • Python Bindings

    Use wavio from Python with familiar APIs. Fingerprint files, build indices, and query tracks.

    Python Guide

  • Rust Library

    Full control over the DSP pipeline. Zero-cost abstractions, no unsafe code.

    Rust Guide

  • CLI Tool

    Index and query audio from the command line. Batch process entire folders.

    CLI Reference

  • Performance

    88ms to fingerprint a 3-min track. 0.57µs per query. No GPU required.

    Benchmarks

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Audio File (.wav)
  ↓  load & normalize (mono f32 @ 22,050 Hz)
    ↓  sliding-window FFT (Hann, 2048-sample frames)
      ↓  dB power spectrogram
        ↓  2D local-max peak detection
          ↓  combinatorial hashing (peak pairs → u64)
            ↓  index  →  query  →  match!

Two recordings of the same song — even with background noise — share a large subset of their spectral peaks. The query engine finds the track whose hash times align best via a time-offset histogram, and returns the match with its score and position.

docs.title: Parallelism (rayon) & Benchmarking (criterion)
docs.text:
• Gated parallel processing behind the parallel feature flag.
  • Added extract_peaks_parallel to peaks.rs. It distributes frame-level local-max computation across the thread pool (embarrassingly parallel since it's read-only on the spectrogram).
  • Added generate_hashes_parallel to hash.rs to compute each anchor's target pairs independently.
  • Added Index::insert_batch_parallel to index.rs which performs the CPU-heavy DSP fingerprinting concurrently, then inserts into the HashMap serially. Decided against DashMap as it's unnecessary since only the cheap insertion phase is serial.
  • Created benches/fingerprint.rs with 3 benchmarks: fingerprint_single_3min, index_insert_1k_tracks, and index_query_1k.
  • Baseline numbers recorded in docs/BENCHMARKS.md:
  • ~88.6 ms to fingerprint a 3-minute clip
  • ~1.04 ms to insert 1,000 tracks
  • ~568 µs to perform 1,000 queries (~0.57 µs per query)
• data samples: https://www.mmsp.ece.mcgill.ca/Documents/AudioFormats/WAVE/Samples.html

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text:
The wavio-cli binary provides three subcommands for indexing, querying, and inspecting fingerprint databases.

Installation

cargo build --release --bin wavio-cli --features persist

docs.title: Global Flags
docs.text: Flag Description --verbose, -v Print detailed output (peak count, hash count, timing) --help, -h Show help --version, -V Show version

docs.title: index
docs.text:
Index WAV files into a persistent database.

wavio-cli index --db <DB_PATH> <INPUT_PATH>
  • INPUT_PATH can be a single WAV file or a directory
  • When given a directory, indexes all .wav files found
  • If the database already exists, new tracks are added to it

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Index a single file
wavio-cli index --db music.db song.wav

# Index an entire folder
wavio-cli index --db music.db ./music/

# Verbose — see hash counts per track
wavio-cli --verbose index --db music.db ./music/
# Indexed 'hotel_california': 4521 hashes
# Indexed 'bohemian_rhapsody': 6832 hashes
# ...

A progress bar is shown during batch indexing.

docs.title: query
docs.text:
Identify an audio clip against the database.

wavio-cli query --db <DB_PATH> <FILE>

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Match found: hotel_california
Score: 312
Confidence: 87.3%
Margin over runner-up: 62.0%
Offset: 47.35s

Options: --min-confidence <F> and --min-margin <F> turn weak matches into "no match"; --detect-speed also prints Estimated speed: 1.04x.

docs.title: Hashing modes
docs.text:
--hybrid (pairwise + triplet hashes; best overall, ~1.5x index size) and --robust (triplet only) are global flags. The database records the settings it was built with, so querying or extending it with a different mode fails with Incompatible index rather than silently finding nothing. index --force replaces tracks that are already present.

If no match is found:

No match found.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This guide walks through the core workflow: fingerprint → index → query.

docs.title: 1. Fingerprint an audio file
docs.text:
import wavio

fp = wavio.PyFingerprinter()
hashes = fp.fingerprint_file("song.wav")
print(f"Generated {len(hashes)} fingerprints")
# Generated 4521 fingerprints

Each fingerprint is a (hash: int, anchor_time: float) tuple.

docs.title: 2. Build an index
docs.text:
index = wavio.PyIndex()
index.insert("Song A", fp.fingerprint_file("song_a.wav"))
index.insert("Song B", fp.fingerprint_file("song_b.wav"))
index.insert("Song C", fp.fingerprint_file("song_c.wav"))

print(f"{index.track_count} tracks, {index.hash_count} hashes")

docs.title: 3. Query a clip
docs.text:
clip_hashes = fp.fingerprint_file("clip.wav")
result = index.query(clip_hashes)

if result:
    print(f"Match: {result['track_id']}")
    print(f"Score: {result['score']}")
    print(f"Offset: {result['offset_secs']:.1f}s into the track")
else:
    print("No match found.")

docs.title: 4. Save and load (optional)
docs.text:
# Save for later
index.save("music.db")

# In a new session
index = wavio.PyIndex.load("music.db")

docs.title: 1. Fingerprint an audio file
docs.text:
use wavio::dsp::audio::load_wav;
use wavio::dsp::spectrogram::{compute_spectrogram, SpectrogramConfig};
use wavio::dsp::peaks::{extract_peaks, PeakExtractorConfig};
use wavio::hash::{generate_hashes, HashConfig};

fn fingerprint(path: &str) -> Vec<wavio::hash::Fingerprint> {
    let audio = load_wav(path).expect("failed to load");
    let spec = compute_spectrogram(&audio.samples, &SpectrogramConfig::default()).unwrap();
    let peaks = extract_peaks(&spec, &PeakExtractorConfig::default());
    generate_hashes(&peaks, &HashConfig::default())
}

let hashes = fingerprint("song.wav");
println!("{} fingerprints", hashes.len());

docs.title: 2. Build an index
docs.text:
use wavio::index::Index;

let mut index = Index::default();
index.insert("Song A", &fingerprint("song_a.wav"));
index.insert("Song B", &fingerprint("song_b.wav"));

println!("{} tracks, {} hashes", index.track_count(), index.hash_count());

docs.title: 3. Query a clip
docs.text:
let clip = fingerprint("clip.wav");

match index.query(&clip) {
    Some(result) => {
        println!("Match: {}", result.track_id);
        println!("Score: {}", result.score);
        println!("Offset: {:.1}s", result.offset_secs);
    }
    None => println!("No match found."),
}

docs.title: 4. Save and load (optional, requires persist feature)
docs.text:
// Save
index.save_to_disk("./music.db")?;

// Load
let index = Index::load_from_disk("./music.db")?;

docs.title: Python Guide
docs.text: wavio provides Python bindings via PyO3 — the fingerprinting runs in Rust at native speed while exposing a Pythonic API.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Python API has two classes:

Class Purpose PyFingerprinter Extracts fingerprints from WAV files PyIndex Stores and queries fingerprints 
import wavio

# The two classes you need
fp = wavio.PyFingerprinter()
index = wavio.PyIndex()

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• GIL release — fingerprinting runs without holding the Python GIL, so it's safe to use with threads
  • Native speed — the DSP pipeline runs in compiled Rust, not Python
  • Simple types — fingerprints are plain list[tuple[int, float]], query results are dict

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
import wavio

fp = wavio.PyFingerprinter()
index = wavio.PyIndex()

# Fingerprint and index tracks
for song in ["song_a.wav", "song_b.wav", "song_c.wav"]:
    name = song.replace(".wav", "")
    hashes = fp.fingerprint_file(song)
    index.insert(name, hashes)
    print(f"  ✓ {name}: {len(hashes)} hashes")

# Query
result = index.query(fp.fingerprint_file("mystery_clip.wav"))
if result:
    print(f"It's {result['track_id']}! (score: {result['score']})")

Extracts audio fingerprints from WAV files.

docs.title: fingerprint_file(path: str) -> list[tuple[int, float]]
docs.text:
Loads a WAV file and returns a list of (hash, anchor_time) pairs.

  • The GIL is released during computation — safe for multi-threaded use.
  • Returns an empty list if the audio is too short or contains no detectable peaks.
fp = wavio.PyFingerprinter()
hashes = fp.fingerprint_file("song.wav")
# [(14829304838, 0.023), (9923847123, 0.046), ...]

print(f"Got {len(hashes)} fingerprints")

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description path str Path to a WAV file

Returns: list[tuple[int, float]] — list of (hash, anchor_time_seconds) pairs.

docs.title: Music Library Indexer
docs.text:
Index an entire folder of WAV files and identify clips against it.

import os
import wavio

def build_index(music_dir: str, db_path: str):
    """Index all WAV files in a directory."""
    fp = wavio.PyFingerprinter()
    index = wavio.PyIndex()

    wav_files = [f for f in os.listdir(music_dir) if f.endswith(".wav")]
    print(f"Indexing {len(wav_files)} files...")

    for filename in wav_files:
        path = os.path.join(music_dir, filename)
        track_id = os.path.splitext(filename)[0]
        try:
            hashes = fp.fingerprint_file(path)
            index.insert(track_id, hashes)
            print(f"  ✓ {track_id}: {len(hashes)} hashes")
        except IOError as e:
            print(f"  ✗ {track_id}: {e}")

    index.save(db_path)
    print(f"\nSaved {index.track_count} tracks to {db_path}")


def identify(clip_path: str, db_path: str, min_score: int = 10):
    """Identify a clip against a saved database."""
    fp = wavio.PyFingerprinter()
    index = wavio.PyIndex.load(db_path)

    hashes = fp.fingerprint_file(clip_path)
    result = index.query(hashes)

    if result and result["score"] >= min_score:
        print(f"Match: {result['track_id']}")
        print(f"Offset: {result['offset_secs']:.1f}s  (score: {result['score']})")
    else:
        print("No confident match found.")


# Usage
build_index("./music/", "./music.db")
identify("./clip.wav", "./music.db")

docs.title: Batch Fingerprinting with Threading
docs.text:
The GIL is released during fingerprinting, so you can safely use threads:

import wavio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

fp = wavio.PyFingerprinter()
files = ["song_a.wav", "song_b.wav", "song_c.wav", "song_d.wav"]

def process(path):
    name = path.replace(".wav", "")
    hashes = fp.fingerprint_file(path)  # GIL released here
    return name, hashes

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(process, files))

index = wavio.PyIndex()
for name, hashes in results:
    index.insert(name, hashes)

print(f"Indexed {index.track_count} tracks")

docs.title: Query with Confidence Threshold
docs.text:
In production, always filter on score to avoid false positives:

import wavio

def identify(clip_path: str, db_path: str):
    fp = wavio.PyFingerprinter()
    index = wavio.PyIndex.load(db_path)
    hashes = fp.fingerprint_file(clip_path)
    result = index.query(hashes)

    if result is None:
        return {"status": "no_match"}

    if result["score"] < 10:
        return {"status": "low_confidence", "candidate": result["track_id"]}

    return {
        "status": "match",
        "track": result["track_id"],
        "score": result["score"],
        "position": f"{result['offset_secs']:.1f}s",
    }

docs.title: Django / Flask Integration
docs.text:
# views.py (Django example)
import wavio
import tempfile

# Load index once at startup
INDEX = wavio.PyIndex.load("/data/music.db")
FP = wavio.PyFingerprinter()

def identify_upload(request):
    audio_file = request.FILES["clip"]

    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".wav", delete=True) as tmp:
        for chunk in audio_file.chunks():
            tmp.write(chunk)
        tmp.flush()

        hashes = FP.fingerprint_file(tmp.name)
        result = INDEX.query(hashes)

    if result and result["score"] > 10:
        return JsonResponse({"track": result["track_id"], "score": result["score"]})
    return JsonResponse({"track": None}, status=404)

docs.title: Internal Sample Rate: 22,050 Hz
docs.text:
• Nyquist frequency of 11,025 Hz — sufficient for music fingerprinting
  • Half the samples of 44,100 Hz — faster processing
  • Standard in audio fingerprinting research

Defined as INTERNAL_SAMPLE_RATE in dsp/audio.rs.

docs.title: FFT Size: 2048 samples
docs.text:
• Frequency resolution: ~10.77 Hz per bin (22,050 / 2,048)
  • Time resolution per frame: ~23.2 ms (512 / 22,050) with hop=512

4096-sample FFT was considered but doubles compute cost with diminishing returns for music identification.

docs.title: Hash Bit-Packing Layout
docs.text:
Bits 40–59   Bits 20–39   Bits 0–19
┌────────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
│ freq1_bin  │ freq2_bin  │  delta_t   │
│  (20 bits) │  (20 bits) │  (20 bits) │
└────────────┴────────────┴────────────┘

20 bits per field supports up to 1,048,575 values. Packing into u64 makes hashing and HashMap lookups trivially fast.

docs.title: Offset Histogram Query
docs.text:
1. For each query hash found in the index, compute offset = db_time - query_time
  2. Quantize offset into bins (default 50 ms)
  3. Track with tallest histogram bin wins

docs.title: Persistence: redb
docs.text:
Embedded, transactional, pure-Rust key-value store with a B-tree storage layout and ACID guarantees. Four redb tables:

Table Key Value hashes u64 bincode Vec<(TrackId, f32)> tracks_by_name track name u32 ID tracks_by_id u32 ID track name metadata "config", "next_id" config / counter

redb replaced the originally-planned sled backend (which was in maintenance mode) before the v0.1 release.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
1. Time stretching & pitch shifting. Significant tempo changes (>5%) or pitch shifts break hash matching — see ARCHITECTURE.md for details.
  2. Linear-interpolation resampling. Non-native sample rates are resampled to 22,050 Hz without an anti-aliasing low-pass filter, which can introduce minor aliasing artifacts for heavily downsampled sources.
  3. No concurrent writes. The Index uses a plain HashMap; concurrent mutation requires external synchronization. insert_batch_parallel parallelizes fingerprint computation upstream, not the insertion itself.
  4. Music-tuned defaults. Speech or environmental audio may need parameter tuning.

docs.title: wavio Benchmarks
docs.text:
Platform: Linux x86-64, 12 hardware threads, powersave CPU governor, desktop in use. Release profile (lto = true, codegen-units = 1). Criterion, sample_size(10) for the heavy groups. Run-to-run noise on this machine is about ±20%; compare orders of magnitude and A/B ratios, not the last digit.

The previous baseline (macOS, 2026-03) used toy workloads (20-hash tracks, a pure sine for DSP), which measured almost nothing: a pure sine yields almost no peaks, and a 20-hash track is ~0.04% of a real one. It is replaced by the sizes below.

Every query in the benchmarks is asserted to return the correct track before it is timed.

A/B method for the entries compared with 0.3.0: both versions were built from the same benchmark file (a throwaway git worktree of the previous commit), run alternately three times, and compared by median. Results that moved less than the noise (serial peak extraction, in-memory and on-disk query) are reported as unchanged; the new adjacent-bin scoring and the multimap layout cost no measurable query time.

What did not work: a separable max-filter for peak picking benchmarked at 267 ms serial / 56 ms parallel vs ~114 / ~35 ms for the early-exit scan, so it was reverted.

docs.title: Reading the table
docs.text:
• pairwise is the best in noise but is useless once audio is sped up or slowed down.
  • triplet survives speed changes but is the weakest in heavy noise; sub-bin frequency interpolation fixes most of its speed fragility (+2%, 3 s: 85% → 98%).
  • hybrid keeps pairwise's noise robustness and triplet's speed robustness (0 dB noise, 3 s: 98%; +-6% speed: 92-95%), at ~1.5x the hashes of pairwise.
  • time-scale voting doesn't raise accuracy, but its speed estimate is accurate (last line).
  • The remaining misses are short (3 s) clips combining noise and speed change (80%); at 5-10 s everything above 92%.

docs.title: Real recordings
docs.text:
scripts/prepare_real_eval.sh /usr/share/sounds/ubuntu/ringtones data/real_eval then cargo run --release --features parallel --example 06_accuracy_eval -- --dir data/real_eval

20 real stereo 44.1 kHz recordings (Ubuntu's bundled ringtones; 247 s total; many are short loops, which is itself a hard case for alignment). Queries of 2, 3 and 5 s are cut from the originals, converted to 48 kHz by ffmpeg, optionally MP3-encoded, then loaded and resampled by wavio, so the library (44.1 → 22.05 kHz) and the query (44.1 → 48 → 22.05 kHz) take different resampling paths. Cells pool all three clip lengths: 60 queries per cell, so differences under ~8 points are not significant. Sinc resampler.

Distortion pairwise pairwise + idf triplet + interp triplet + interp + idf hybrid hybrid + idf 48 kHz clean 100% 100% 100% 100% 100% 100% MP3 128 kbps 100% 100% 100% 100% 100% 100% MP3 32 kbps 100% 100% 98% 100% 100% 100% + noise 10 dB 93% 93% 27% 37% 83% 87% + noise 0 dB 60% 62% 12% 15% 52% 55% + speed +3% 18% 10% 100% 100% 100% 100%

Resampler comparison (same data, linear vs sinc; all other rows identical or within one query): hybrid 10 dB noise 80% → 83%, hybrid 0 dB noise 40% → 52%, pairwise unchanged (93% / 60%).

What this changed about earlier conclusions:

  • The synthetic library overstated noise robustness (pairwise at 0 dB: 100% synthetic, 60% real) and triplet-only is far weaker in real noise than synthetic data suggested.
  • Hybrid's edge over pairwise is speed/pitch robustness, not noise: under noise alone pairwise is as good (93% vs 83-87%, not significant) at two-thirds of the index size.
  • MP3 compression, even at 32 kbps, is a non-issue for every mode.
  • IDF weighting never hurts and helps the coarse-hash modes under noise by a few points.
  • The sinc resampler is a correctness fix; its accuracy effect on this data is within noise.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Hybrid hashing (Fingerprinter::with_hybrid_hashing, CLI --hybrid, Python mode="hybrid") — emits pairwise and triplet hashes into one index (triplet hashes carry triplet::TRIPLET_TAG so the families never collide). Pairwise hashes are the most noise-robust but collapse under speed/pitch change; triplet hashes survive speed/pitch change but are weaker in heavy noise. Their votes add in the same offset bin, so whichever survives carries the match. On the synthetic accuracy harness, 3 s clips at 0 dB noise: 98% (hybrid) vs 42–52% (triplet) vs 100% (pairwise); at +-6% speed: 92% vs 78–90% vs 5%. Cost: ~1.5x hashes per track.
  • Sub-bin peak interpolation (PeakExtractorConfig::interpolate, Fingerprinter::with_peak_interpolation) — refines each peak's frequency with a parabolic fit. Off by default so existing hashes are unchanged. It removes most of the FFT-bin quantization error that ratio-based triplet hashes are sensitive to: 3 s clips at +2% speed go from 85% to 98% top-1 accuracy, noise+speed from 55% to 80%. Time is deliberately not interpolated — measured, it made triplet matching much worse. wavio-cli --robust now enables it.
  • Time-scale-aware voting (Index::query_scaled, PersistentIndex::query_scaled, ScaleSearch, CLI query --detect-speed, Python query_scaled) — re-scores the top candidates under a grid of speed hypotheses and reports the estimated speed in the new QueryResult::speed (e.g. a 1.06x clip is reported as 1.06). Opt-in. It does not measurably improve identification accuracy in the benchmark; its value is the speed estimate.
  • QueryResult::margin — lead over the runner-up as a fraction of the winning score. Unlike confidence it does not shrink just because the query contains audio that is not in the index. CLI: query --min-margin <F>; Python: "margin" in the result dict.
  • Fingerprinter::signature() — a stable description of every setting that affects the hashes.
  • PersistentIndex: insert_many (one transaction), remove_track, contains_track, signature / check_signature / ensure_signature, config / set_config. Index::signature / set_signature, Index::insert_batch.
  • WavioError::IncompatibleIndex.
  • examples/06_accuracy_eval.rs — an accuracy harness (top-1 accuracy by hashing mode x clip length x distortion). The library is synthetic, so use it for relative comparisons and regressions, not as an absolute leaderboard.

  • Criterion benchmarks sized like a real library (~10M-entry index, 10 s noisy query clips, 3-minute multi-tone track) instead of 20-hash toy tracks.

  • Windowed-sinc resampler (dsp::audio::resample). The old linear interpolation had no low-pass filter, so downsampling 44.1/48 kHz audio folded everything above 11.025 kHz back into the band. The new Kaiser-windowed-sinc filter removes it (15 kHz tone at 44.1 kHz: alias RMS < 0.01 vs > 0.2), has a flat passband with no added delay, and keeps levels correct at the edges. The old behavior remains as resample_linear. Cost: ~80-90 ms per 3-minute track serial (linear: ~25 ms); with the parallel feature the output samples are computed across threads, bit-identical to serial, at ~17-21 ms. Measured effect on identification accuracy over 20 real recordings is within noise (see BENCHMARKS.md); it is correctness, not a benchmark win.

  • Rarity (IDF) weighting (QueryOptions::idf_weighting, Index::query_with, PersistentIndex::query_with, CLI query --idf, Python idf=True) — each vote is weighted by 1 / (1 + ln(postings)), so hashes that occur in many places (coarse triplet ratios, looping music) count for less. QueryResult::weighted_score reports the ranking score; score stays the raw count of aligned hashes. On real recordings it helps the weaker modes under noise (triplet at 10 dB: 27% -> 37%, hybrid: 83% -> 87%) and is neutral otherwise. Off by default.
  • Real-recording evaluation (examples/06_accuracy_eval.rs --dir DIR, scripts/prepare_real_eval.sh) — builds the library from real audio and sends query clips through the realistic path: cut from the original, converted to 48 kHz and optionally MP3-encoded by ffmpeg, then loaded and resampled by wavio. It showed that the synthetic harness was optimistic (see below).
  • Python bindings parity: PyFingerprinter(mode="pairwise"|"triplet"|"hybrid"), fingerprint_samples (NumPy / array('f') / list, GIL released), PyStreamingFingerprinter, PyPersistentIndex, signature / ensure_fingerprinter / check_fingerprinter, contains_track, idf= on every query, and margin / speed / weighted_score in result dicts. Settings mismatches raise ValueError. 17 pytest tests, now run in CI.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• On-disk format (schema version 2). The hashes table (one bincode Vec per hash, rewritten whole on every insert) is replaced by a postings multimap. Appending a fingerprint is now O(log n) regardless of how many tracks share the hash: inserting a 50,000-hash track takes ~36 ms instead of ~290 ms. Databases from 0.3.0 and earlier are migrated automatically on first open; databases written by this version cannot be opened by older releases. Identical (hash, track, time) entries are stored once, so saving an index twice no longer duplicates anything.
  • The database now records the settings it was built with (hash mode, FFT/peak/hash parameters) and wavio-cli refuses to query or extend it with different ones (Incompatible index: ...). Previously, mixing --robust with a pairwise database silently returned "no match". Databases from before this release have no recorded settings; the CLI warns and assumes they match.
  • PersistentIndex::query* now reads only the postings for the query's hashes straight from disk. wavio-cli no longer loads the whole database into RAM and rewrites it on every index / query run; index fingerprints in parallel and writes all new tracks in a single transaction.
  • A corrupt stored IndexConfig is now an error instead of silently falling back to the default.
  • Scoring: a track's score is its tallest pair of adjacent offset bins (votes straddling a bin boundary are no longer split), the offset is the vote-weighted mean of those bins, and ties are broken deterministically. Index::query, query_topn, PersistentIndex::query and query_topn now share a single implementation (they had been four copies).
  • Index::save_to_disk is O(total entries) (it was O(tracks x entries)) and stores the index config and settings signature.
  • extract_peaks / extract_peaks_parallel share one per-frame implementation; the parallel version is ~40% faster (35 -> 20 ms on a 3-minute track). The serial version is unchanged in speed. (A separable max-filter was tried and benchmarked ~2x slower, because the early-exit scan only pays the full window for actual peaks.)
  • cargo fmt and cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings are clean (CI enforces both).

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text: • Index::insert_batch_parallel — it never ran in parallel. Use Index::insert_batch.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• .github/workflows/pypi.yml built with default features, which produced a bindings-free cffi wheel; it now builds the PyO3 extension (--features python,persist,parallel). Note: the name wavio on PyPI is held by an unrelated project, so the upload step cannot succeed until the package is renamed.
  • wavio-cli index re-run on the same folder with --force duplicated every hash of the re-indexed tracks (load, append, save); --force now replaces them.
  • A multi-channel stream with more than 65,535 channels could silently truncate the channel count in the symphonia decoder.

docs.title: Findings from real recordings
docs.text:
20 real recordings (Ubuntu's bundled ringtones, 247 s total), 60 queries per cell, so differences under ~8 points are not significant:

  • The synthetic harness overstated noise robustness: pairwise at 0 dB noise is 60% on real audio, not 100%. Triplet-only is far worse in noise on real audio (10 dB: ~27%) than on synthetic (90-100%).
  • Hybrid is not strictly better than pairwise. Under noise alone it is statistically indistinguishable from pairwise (83-87% vs 93% at 10 dB), at 1.5x the index size; its advantage is speed/pitch robustness (100% vs 18% at +3% speed). The README now recommends hybrid when speed or pitch changes are possible, pairwise otherwise.
  • MP3 compression is harmless: even 32 kbps scores 98-100% in every mode.
  • The new resampler and IDF weighting are each worth at most a few points; neither hurts any mode.

docs.title: Tried and rejected
docs.text:
Recorded so nobody repeats them; all were measured with examples/06_accuracy_eval.rs:

  • Interpolating peak time as well as frequency: turns frame-aligned peaks into near-coincident ones whose time ratios are pure jitter; accuracy fell sharply (e.g. +2% speed, 3 s: 90% -> 50%).
  • All-pairs triplets (every pair among the nearest candidates rather than adjacent ones): no gain on any distortion and worse on noise, at ~2x the hashes.
  • Coarser triplet ratio quantization (0.02-0.05 log2 steps) and a minimum anchor distance (min_dt = 0.1): both worse on speed and noise.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Pitch-shift / time-stretch-robust hashing (wavio::triplet) — a new opt-in hashing mode that encodes ratios within a triplet of peaks instead of absolute frequency/time values, making it largely invariant to uniform pitch shift and time stretch (see ARCHITECTURE.md §3b for the invariance rationale and its limitations). Enable via Fingerprinter::with_triplet_hashing(TripletHashConfig::default()) or the CLI's new --robust flag. Produces plain Fingerprints, so Index/PersistentIndex require no changes.
  • Streaming fingerprinting (wavio::dsp::streaming::StreamingFingerprinter) — fingerprints audio in overlapping fixed-size blocks so callers don't need the whole file in memory (e.g. live/incremental sources). Block boundaries are aligned to the spectrogram's hop-size grid and trimmed on both edges for full peak-neighborhood and fan-out context, so streamed output matches a single batch Fingerprinter::fingerprint call almost exactly.
  • Index::query_topn / PersistentIndex::query_topn — returns up to n ranked matches (best first) instead of only the single best track.
  • Index::query_with_min_confidence / PersistentIndex::query_with_min_confidence — rejects a match whose confidence is below a threshold.
  • Index::contains_track — checks whether a track name is already indexed.
  • CLI: index --force re-indexes a track already present in the database (previously, re-running index on the same folder silently duplicated every hash for re-indexed tracks); query --min-confidence <F> rejects weak matches; --robust (global) switches both subcommands to triplet hashing.
  • Python bindings: PyIndex.query_topn and PyIndex.query_with_min_confidence, mirroring the new Index methods.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • QueryResult.confidence — score normalized by the query's fingerprint count, giving a [0.0, 1.0]-ish indicator of match decisiveness independent of clip length. Exposed through Index::query, PersistentIndex::query, the CLI (Confidence: NN.N%), and the Python bindings' query dict.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: All DSP parameters are controlled via configuration structs. Each has a Default implementation with sensible values tuned for music.

docs.title: SpectrogramConfig
docs.text:
Controls the FFT spectrogram.

Field Default Tune when… window_size 2048 Need more frequency detail → increase. Need more time detail → decrease. hop_size 512 Smaller = more frames (slower, finer resolution). Larger = faster, coarser. 
let config = SpectrogramConfig {
    window_size: 4096,  // better frequency resolution
    hop_size: 1024,     // fewer frames
};

Power-of-two window sizes

window_size should be a power of two (512, 1024, 2048, 4096) for optimal FFT performance.

docs.title: PeakExtractorConfig
docs.text:
Controls constellation peak detection.

Field Default Tune when… time_neighborhood 10 Larger = sparser peaks (faster queries, less recall) freq_neighborhood 10 Larger = sparser peaks in frequency dimension threshold_db -40.0 Too many peaks → raise threshold. Too few → lower it. sample_rate 22_050 Must match your audio's sample rate hop_size 512 Must match SpectrogramConfig.hop_size window_size 2048 Must match SpectrogramConfig.window_size

Keep configs in sync

sample_rate, hop_size, and window_size in PeakExtractorConfig must match your SpectrogramConfig and actual audio sample rate. Mismatched values will produce incorrect time/frequency coordinates.

Target: 200–500 peaks per 10 seconds of audio.

docs.title: HashConfig
docs.text:
Controls combinatorial hashing of peak pairs.

Field Default Tune when… fan_value 15 More pairs → better recall, more hashes, slower min_dt 0.0 Set > 0 to skip very close peaks max_dt 1.0 Wider window → more hashes, higher collision rate freq_bins 1024 Number of quantization bins for frequency freq_resolution ~10.77 Hz per bin (derived from sample_rate / window_size) dt_resolution 0.01 Time quantization step in seconds

Target: 1,000–5,000 hashes per track.

docs.title: IndexConfig
docs.text:
Controls the query time-offset histogram.

Field Default Tune when… offset_bin_size 0.05 Smaller = finer offset resolution, lower peak height. Larger = more robust.

docs.title: Recommended Defaults
docs.text:
The defaults work well for pop/rock music at standard sample rates. Use custom configs for:

Use case Changes to try Speech threshold_db: -30.0, max_dt: 2.0, fan_value: 10 Noisy environment threshold_db: -25.0, time_neighborhood: 15 Short clips (< 5s) fan_value: 20, offset_bin_size: 0.01 Large database (10k+ tracks) fan_value: 10 (reduces hash count)

docs.title: Rust Guide
docs.text: wavio is a native Rust library with zero unsafe code. It gives you full control over every stage of the DSP pipeline.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The library is organized into modules that mirror the pipeline:

wavio::dsp::audio       →  Load WAV, normalize to mono f32
wavio::dsp::spectrogram →  Sliding-window FFT → dB spectrogram
wavio::dsp::peaks       →  2D local-max peak extraction
wavio::hash             →  Combinatorial hashing → u64 fingerprints
wavio::index            →  In-memory index + query engine
wavio::persist          →  On-disk redb backend (feature = "persist")
wavio::io               →  Pluggable audio source trait
wavio::error            →  WavioError enum

docs.title: Minimal Example
docs.text:
use wavio::dsp::audio::load_wav;
use wavio::dsp::spectrogram::{compute_spectrogram, SpectrogramConfig};
use wavio::dsp::peaks::{extract_peaks, PeakExtractorConfig};
use wavio::hash::{generate_hashes, HashConfig};
use wavio::index::Index;

let audio = load_wav("track.wav").unwrap();
let spec = compute_spectrogram(&audio.samples, &SpectrogramConfig::default()).unwrap();
let peaks = extract_peaks(&spec, &PeakExtractorConfig::default());
let hashes = generate_hashes(&peaks, &HashConfig::default());

let mut index = Index::default();
index.insert("track", &hashes);

docs.title: Helper: Fingerprint function

Most examples reuse this helper:

use wavio::dsp::audio::load_wav;
use wavio::dsp::spectrogram::{compute_spectrogram, SpectrogramConfig};
use wavio::dsp::peaks::{extract_peaks, PeakExtractorConfig};
use wavio::hash::{generate_hashes, Fingerprint, HashConfig};

fn fingerprint(path: &str) -> Result<Vec<Fingerprint>, wavio::error::WavioError> {
    let audio = load_wav(path)?;
    let spec = compute_spectrogram(&audio.samples, &SpectrogramConfig::default())?;
    let peaks = extract_peaks(&spec, &PeakExtractorConfig::default());
    Ok(generate_hashes(&peaks, &HashConfig::default()))
}

docs.title: Index and Query
docs.text:
use wavio::index::Index;

fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let mut index = Index::default();

    // Index a library
    for path in &["song_a.wav", "song_b.wav", "song_c.wav"] {
        let name = path.replace(".wav", "");
        let hashes = fingerprint(path)?;
        println!("  ✓ {name}: {} hashes", hashes.len());
        index.insert(&name, &hashes);
    }

    // Query
    let clip = fingerprint("clip.wav")?;
    match index.query(&clip) {
        Some(r) => println!("Match: {} (score {}, offset {:.1}s)", r.track_id, r.score, r.offset_secs),
        None => println!("No match."),
    }

    Ok(())
}

docs.title: Parallel Batch Indexing
docs.text:
Requires the parallel feature.

use rayon::prelude::*;
use wavio::index::Index;

fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let files = vec!["a.wav", "b.wav", "c.wav", "d.wav"];

    // Fingerprint in parallel
    let batch: Vec<(String, Vec<_>)> = files
        .par_iter()
        .filter_map(|path| {
            let name = path.replace(".wav", "");
            fingerprint(path).ok().map(|h| (name, h))
        })
        .collect();

    // Insert (serial, cheap)
    let mut index = Index::default();
    for (name, hashes) in &batch {
        index.insert(name, hashes);
    }

    println!("{} tracks indexed", index.track_count());
    Ok(())
}

use wavio::dsp::audio::load_wav;
use wavio::dsp::spectrogram::{compute_spectrogram, SpectrogramConfig};
use wavio::dsp::peaks::{extract_peaks, PeakExtractorConfig};
use wavio::hash::{generate_hashes, HashConfig};

    window_size: 4096,
    hop_size: 1024,

    threshold_db: -30.0,
    time_neighborhood: 15,
    freq_neighborhood: 15,
    window_size: 4096,  // must match spectrogram
    hop_size: 1024,     // must match spectrogram
    ..PeakExtractorConfig::default()
};
let peaks = extract_peaks(&spec, &peak_config);

// Wider time window for speech
let hash_config = HashConfig {
    max_dt: 2.0,
    fan_value: 10,
    ..HashConfig::default()

let hashes = generate_hashes(&peaks, &hash_config);
